scope: All 27 HKDSE English Language Paper 4 sets for 2016

methodology.primary_evidence: Complete 27-page examination scan; one examiner sheet per set, visually checked for Part A task, discussion points and Part B printed order.
methodology.copyright_treatment: Official context articles were used only to establish topic and scenario. Every replacement is an original 3–4 paragraph practice text in a natural source genre and contains no candidate-facing meta-instructions.

global_findings: All 27 set numbers and topics are supported by the examination scan.
The existing Part A discussion points are substantively accurate, but the generic instruction often removes the actual task type and scenario.
Part B order is wrong in 24 of 27 sets. Sets 9.1, 9.2 and 9.3 are already in printed order.
All 27 Contexts have been rewritten as natural, topic-specific practice texts; none reproduces an official source article or includes candidate-facing discussion instructions.
Stable point_id and question_id values are preserved. The replacement changes display order without reassigning semantic identity.

records.title: Charity Work Outside Hong Kong
records.source_note: 2016 Paper 4 set identity, Part A task and Part B printed order cross-referenced against a complete examination scan and two independent public indexes. Context is a newly written practice adaptation, not official examination text.

context.source_line: Original practice context written in an HKDSE-style source genre; it is not the official 2016 examination text.
context.title: Practice context: Charity Work Outside Hong Kong
body: A Hong Kong secondary school is considering an overseas service trip in which students would help a community organisation with teaching, repairs and daily activities. The trip would expose students to living conditions different from their own, but each participant would have to pay for travel and accommodation.

Supporters believe direct service can build empathy, teamwork and a stronger understanding of global inequality. Critics question whether a short visit creates lasting benefit, whether students are properly trained and whether the money might be better spent supporting local charities.

The proposed seven-day visit would combine classroom support with practical jobs such as painting community facilities. A partner charity would supervise the work, arrange child-protection training and explain which projects local residents have requested.

The school must decide whether overseas service should become a graduation requirement. Subsidies could widen access, while a local alternative might help students who cannot travel and ensure that volunteering is motivated by service rather than a certificate.

part_a.instruction: Your group is discussing the kinds of charity work your school could be involved in. You may want to talk about:

discussion_points.text: The benefits of students doing charity work outside Hong Kong
The concerns of doing charity work outside Hong Kong
Whether charity work outside Hong Kong should be a requirement at secondary school
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: Have you ever done any charity work?
Would you prefer to do charity work locally or overseas?
Do you think it's important to donate money to charity?
Which is more important: giving money or giving your time?
Do you think it is necessary to leave Hong Kong to do charity work?
Should students have to pay to do charity work outside Hong Kong?
Do you think charity work can really make a difference?
Who benefits more from charity work outside Hong Kong—the volunteers or the local communities?

context.title: Practice context: Starting Your Own Business
body: Many Hong Kong homes have limited storage space. A new business proposes delivering secure boxes to customers, collecting them after packing, keeping an online inventory and returning individual items on request. Customers would pay a monthly fee rather than rent a larger flat.

The service may be convenient for seasonal clothes, books and keepsakes, yet customers may worry about price, privacy, damage and the time needed to retrieve an item. A successful company would also need reliable collection, transparent insurance and advertising that explains why it is better than self-storage.

Spacebox would photograph and label every container before moving it to a warehouse. Users could request next-day delivery through an app, although urgent access and oversized objects would cost extra under the proposed price plan.

The founders are considering student discounts, shared family accounts and reusable packing materials. Before launching, they need to prove that the warehouse is secure and that customers can understand insurance limits, collection times and cancellation charges.

part_a.instruction: As members of an extra-curricular course called “Starting Your Own Business”, your group has been asked to decide whether it would be worthwhile starting a similar business to Spacebox. You may want to talk about:

discussion_points.text: Whether Spacebox is a good business idea
Ways the business idea could be improved
Different ways to advertise your business
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: What items would you put inside your Spacebox?

How do you try to create more space in your home?
How could flats in Hong Kong be designed to provide more storage space?
What space-saving tips would you give to someone moving into a small flat in Hong Kong?
Is having fewer possessions the key to a happier life?

records.title: Learning Through Play
records.source_note: 2016 Paper 4 set identity, Part A task and Part B printed order cross-referenced against a complete examination scan and two independent public indexes. Context is a newly written practice adaptation, not official examination text.

context.source_line: Original practice context written in an HKDSE-style source genre; it is not the official 2016 examination text.
context.title: Practice context: Learning Through Play
body: Some educators argue that play is not a break from learning but one of the ways children learn. Building games can develop planning, outdoor exploration can encourage curiosity, and role-play can improve communication. However, Hong Kong schools often have tight timetables and strong pressure to show measurable academic progress.

Teachers must decide how much freedom children should have, what kinds of games are suitable and how learning can be observed without turning every activity into a test. Parents may welcome creative lessons but still worry about safety, discipline and whether play reduces time for reading, writing and mathematics.

One primary school has tested a weekly ninety-minute play session. Pupils choose from construction challenges, drama corners and supervised garden activities, then record what they discovered in a short learning journal.

The pilot has produced lively lessons, but teachers report that large classes make observation difficult. The school is deciding whether to expand the programme, reduce homework on play days and invite parents to see how apparently simple games develop useful skills.

part_a.instruction: Your group is planning to write an essay in class about whether learning through play should be a regular part of education in Hong Kong schools. You may want to talk about:

discussion_points.text: Games that you played when you were younger
The advantages and disadvantages of allowing children to play at school
Whether learning through play should be a regular part of a child's education
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: Do you do any outdoor activities?
Do you think Hong Kong children can easily find places to play?
What toys did you enjoy playing with when you were very young?
Do you enjoy going outdoors and exploring nature?
Do you think it's fun to get dirty while playing?
Should the government provide more indoor playrooms for children?
If you were in charge of a kindergarten class, where would you take the children for a day?
Do you think playing video games is as educational as outdoor play?

records.source_note: 2016 Paper 4 set identity, Part A task and Part B printed order cross-referenced against a complete examination scan and two independent public indexes. Context is a newly written practice adaptation, not official examination text.

context.source_line: Original practice context written in an HKDSE-style source genre; it is not the official 2016 examination text.
context.title: Practice context: Phone Scams
body: Phone and online scams often create a false sense of urgency. A caller may pretend to represent a bank, a message may promise a prize, or an email may appear to come from a friend who needs money. Criminals rely on fear, trust and personal information to make victims act before checking.

Young people are not automatically safe simply because they use technology confidently. Useful precautions include refusing to share passwords, contacting an organisation through an official number and asking a trusted adult for advice. Public education must reach both frequent internet users and people who may be unfamiliar with changing scam methods.

A recent school survey found that suspicious calls were often ignored, but convincing messages from hacked accounts caused more confusion. Several students said they would transfer a small sum if the request appeared to come from a close friend.

The school plans a public-awareness presentation using recorded examples, a verification checklist and a demonstration of caller-ID manipulation. Organisers want advice that protects victims without making people afraid of every unfamiliar message or genuine request for help.

part_a.instruction: Your group is going to give a presentation to your school about how to avoid different kinds of scams. Discuss with your group what to include in your talk. You may want to talk about:

discussion_points.text: The different types of scams
Possible victims of scams
How to avoid being a victim of scams
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: Is it safe to store personal information on a phone?
Have you ever received an unwanted phone call?
Have you or someone you know ever been tricked?

Do you think there is an increasing trend of people being scammed in Hong Kong?
Do you think enough has been done to educate the public about the dangers of scams?
If a friend emailed you asking for help and money, what would you do?
Do you think people who lie always do it to harm others?

context.title: Practice context: Street Art for the School Open Day
body: A school celebrating its anniversary has invited a Hong Kong street artist to paint a mural. Her work uses bold lines, local images and large public walls, so the mural could become a memorable feature of the campus and a focus for the Open Day.

The school must choose a visible but suitable location and decide which images represent its history, values and students. The artist might also give a demonstration or involve students in planning. At the same time, organisers need to consider cost, safety, maintenance and whether the design will remain meaningful after the celebration.

The artist has suggested a wall beside the main entrance, where the work would be visible to visitors but exposed to strong sun and rain. Her first sketch combines the old school building, neighbourhood shops and portraits designed from student photographs.

During Open Day, she could lead a stencil workshop and explain how a mural moves from research to final painting. The anniversary committee must decide how much creative control students should have and who will repair or replace the work in future.

context.title: Practice context: Living with Parents in Your Twenties
body: High housing costs mean many young adults in Hong Kong continue living with their parents after starting work. Staying at home can reduce expenses, allow family members to support one another and make daily life more convenient. It can also reflect a family tradition rather than a failure to become independent.

Sharing a home may nevertheless limit privacy and create disagreements about money, chores, visitors and personal schedules. Independence can still be developed through paying part of the household costs, making decisions responsibly and planning for the future. Families need expectations that respect both the young adult and the parents.

In one household, a working daughter pays rent, cooks twice a week and manages her own savings while sharing a flat with her parents. She values family company but finds it difficult when relatives expect to know all her plans.

Housing advisers say moving out is not the only sign of adulthood. Clear household agreements, private space and long-term financial goals can reduce tension, although both generations must be willing to treat the arrangement as a partnership between adults.

part_a.instruction: Your group is discussing the idea of living at home with your parents when you are in your twenties. You may want to talk about:

anything else you think is important

context.title: Practice context: Educational Apps for Students
body: A school Computer Club has been asked to recommend educational apps for new tablets. Possible choices include tools for practising languages, organising revision, exploring scientific models and checking understanding through quizzes. The most attractive app is not necessarily the one that produces the best learning.

Students should consider price, accessibility, privacy, accuracy and whether an app works without a fast internet connection. Too much screen time may distract learners, while a well-designed app can give immediate feedback and allow practice at an appropriate level. Teachers also need training and a clear purpose for using each tool.

The club has a fixed budget and can purchase only two subscriptions this year. Trial users liked the science model but found it demanding on older tablets; the language app was easier to use, although some feedback was inaccurate.

Members will test each option with students from different forms and collect teachers’ comments before recommending a purchase. They also want an offline mode and a policy that prevents advertising or unnecessary collection of pupils’ personal data.

context.title: Practice context: Complaints against Hong Kong Taxi Drivers
body: Complaints about Hong Kong taxis have increased, with passengers reporting overcharging, refusal of hire and poor behaviour. Because taxis are often used by visitors, one bad journey can damage the city’s reputation as well as trust in the industry. Drivers, however, also face congestion, long hours and rising operating costs.

Improvement could combine fair enforcement with better support. Clear fare information, easier complaint procedures, driver training and recognition for good service may all help. The industry must also respond to competition from app-based hire-car services while ensuring that passengers receive safe, reliable and courteous transport.

The Transport Department is considering mystery-passenger checks and a clearer digital receipt showing the route and fare. Driver groups support action against serious misconduct but want complaints investigated before penalties affect a licence.

Tourism representatives propose a multilingual booking guide and a voluntary service badge for trained drivers. Any reform will need enough taxis at busy times, simple reporting for visitors and rewards that make professional service worth maintaining.

part_a.instruction: As a follow-up on Hong Kong tourism in your English Language class, your group has been asked to discuss the image of Hong Kong taxi drivers and to suggest ways to improve this image. You may want to talk about:

records.source_note: 2016 Paper 4 set identity, Part A task and Part B printed order cross-referenced against a complete examination scan and two independent public indexes. Context is a newly written practice adaptation, not official examination text.

context.title: Practice context: Protecting Wild Animals
body: Wild boars sometimes enter residential areas in search of food. Some residents fear damage or injury and call for the animals to be removed, while conservation groups argue that shooting should be a last resort. Feeding by people and easy access to rubbish can make encounters more frequent.

A balanced policy could include secure bins, public warnings, habitat management and trained teams that move animals away from crowded places. Any decision must consider human safety, animal welfare and the practical limits of non-lethal methods. The debate is about when protection should give way to control.

Wildlife officers have recorded more reports near housing estates after residents left food beside rubbish collection points. Most encounters ended without injury, but frightened animals can behave unpredictably when surrounded or chased for photographs.

A district trial will install animal-proof bins and send trained teams to crowded locations. Officials will review whether these measures reduce conflict before deciding when relocation, fertility control or lethal action can be justified.

context.title: Practice context: Computer Programming in Schools
body: Some schools are considering whether computer programming should receive more curriculum time. Programming can develop logical thinking, creativity and problem-solving, and these skills may be useful in many future jobs. Supporters even suggest reducing time for subjects such as history and geography.

Others argue that students need knowledge of society, place and the past in order to make responsible decisions. Programming may also be difficult to teach well without trained staff and suitable equipment. Schools must decide whether it should begin in primary school and how to balance technical skills with a broad education.

A proposed timetable would give every junior student one programming lesson a week. Rather than memorising code, classes would design simple games, test instructions and explain why a solution failed, but the change would reduce time available for other subjects.

The principal has asked departments to suggest a balanced curriculum. One option links programming with maps, historical data and creative projects, allowing digital skills to support existing subjects instead of replacing the knowledge those subjects provide.

context.title: Practice context: Socialising after School
body: After-school time gives teenagers a chance to relax and maintain friendships, but suitable meeting places can be difficult to find. Libraries are quiet and inexpensive, shopping centres are convenient but crowded, and activity centres may offer useful facilities but close early.

A good hangout should be safe, affordable, accessible and welcoming to young people. It should also allow conversation without disturbing others. Schools and communities may need to provide more spaces, while students must show that socialising can be responsible and does not prevent them from completing homework or family duties.

The Peer Counselling team surveyed students about three possible venues: a covered area on campus, a youth centre and a café offering a group discount. Cost and travel time mattered more to respondents than fashionable decoration.

The team hopes to propose a welcoming space with Wi-Fi, drinking water and some organised activities, while keeping areas for ordinary conversation. Rules on noise, closing time and respectful behaviour would be agreed with students rather than imposed without consultation.

context.title: Practice context: Private Kitchens
body: Private kitchens serve small groups in flats, studios or other spaces rather than in conventional restaurants. Customers may enjoy a personal atmosphere, unusual menus and direct contact with the cook. Operators can test creative ideas without paying for a large dining room.

The model raises concerns about licences, hygiene, fire safety, prices and consumer protection. Neighbours may also be affected by noise or frequent visitors. Private kitchens can add variety to Hong Kong’s food culture, but their success depends on trust, clear standards and honest information about what customers are paying for.

A local cook runs a twelve-seat private kitchen twice a week, serving one seasonal menu announced online. Guests appreciate meeting the chef, but first-time customers say it is difficult to check licences, allergy arrangements and refund terms.

Restaurant owners argue that all food businesses should meet comparable safety requirements. Private-kitchen operators reply that small bookings and limited menus are different from full restaurants. A sensible policy would protect diners without removing the experimentation that attracts them.

body: Buskers bring live music and performance into streets and public spaces. Supporters say they make the city more lively and give new artists a way to meet audiences. A performer can gain experience without first being invited to a concert hall.

Critics complain about noise, repeated songs, blocked walkways and performers who seem to pressure people for money. Improving busking may require suitable locations, reasonable time limits and a fair permit system. The government must encourage creativity without making public performance so controlled that its energy disappears.

A residents’ letter has asked the district to ban amplification after repeated evening performances below nearby flats. Musicians respond that a total restriction would silence skilled performers along with the small number who cause complaints.

The arts committee is considering marked pitches, audition-free registration and quiet hours near homes. It may also publish a public code covering volume, crowd management and voluntary donations, with warnings before a performer loses access to popular locations.

context.title: Practice context: History Week
body: A school plans to hold a History Week and wants one Events Day to bring a chosen period to life. Students could create an exhibition, perform scenes, prepare food, invite a speaker or design an interactive trail around the campus.

The organisers need a period with enough reliable information and features that can be shown respectfully. Activities should do more than provide costumes and decorations; they should help students understand how people lived and why events mattered. Students have shortlisted the 1960s in Hong Kong, the age of maritime trade and the early development of railways. Each choice offers strong visual material, but borrowed objects and specialist speakers would affect the budget.

The Events Day could combine an evidence-based exhibition with oral histories, demonstrations and a problem-solving trail. Teachers want sources clearly labelled so that entertainment supports accurate learning, while organisers hope every class can contribute without repeating the same display.

context.title: Practice context: Electronic Devices and Social Skills
body: Electronic devices help young people study, communicate and organise daily life. Yet constant checking can interrupt face-to-face conversation, reduce attention and make quiet moments uncomfortable. Online contact may keep friendships active, but it does not always develop the same listening and social skills as meeting in person.

Schools and families must decide whether limits are needed and how they can be realistic. Device-free activities, agreed times and better role models may work better than a total ban. The goal is not to reject technology, but to help young people use it without weakening relationships or well-being.

The Student Union observed that lunchtime groups often sat together while every member looked at a separate screen. Students said devices helped arrange meetings, yet notifications continued interrupting conversations after friends had arrived.

A proposed Connection Week would provide phone-free tables, cooperative games and short workshops on attentive listening. Participation would be voluntary, and secure storage would be available, allowing the campaign to demonstrate alternatives instead of treating normal device use as wrongdoing.

context.title: Practice context: A More Walkable Hong Kong
body: Walking in Hong Kong can be difficult when pavements are narrow, crossings are inconvenient and construction or parked objects block the route. Heat, rain, traffic and poor signs also discourage people, especially children, older residents and wheelchair users.

A more walkable city would need shade, seating, safer crossings, connected paths and clear information. A campaign leaflet should identify real obstacles, explain practical improvements and show how walking benefits health, neighbourhood businesses and the environment. Its message must be organised so readers can act on it quickly.

A street audit around the school found missing dropped kerbs, delivery boxes across pavements and crossings that gave slower walkers too little time. Students also mapped shaded routes that already make short journeys pleasant.

The proposed leaflet will pair photographs of obstacles with a neighbourhood walking map and a channel for reporting hazards. Community groups want improvements tested with wheelchair users, parents and older residents before money is spent on decorative features.

context.title: Practice context: Singapore-style Public Conduct Laws
body: Singapore is known for strict public-conduct rules, including controls on littering, eating in some transport areas and the sale of chewing gum. Some people believe similar rules could make Hong Kong cleaner and more orderly. Others worry that copying penalties ignores differences between the two cities.

Effective rules must be understandable, proportionate and enforced consistently. Heavy fines may discourage behaviour, but they can also seem unfair if public facilities or education are inadequate. The government should consider whether each proposed law solves a genuine problem and whether less severe measures could work.

The proposal includes higher littering fines, restrictions on food in public transport and tighter control of chewing gum sales. Supporters expect visible rules to change habits quickly; civil-rights groups ask how warnings, appeals and enforcement records would work.

Officials will compare cleanliness data, enforcement costs and the effect on visitors before recommending legislation. They are also considering more bins and public education, because punishment may have little effect when facilities are inconvenient or rules appear arbitrary.

Designers favour tiled walls and compact booth seating rather than filling the room with unrelated souvenirs. Local suppliers would prepare fresh ingredients, while guest events featuring music, illustration and travel stories could keep the theme changing after the opening publicity ends.

context.title: Practice context: Trophies for Losing Teams
body: Some schools give trophies to every child who takes part in a competition. Supporters say this protects confidence, recognises effort and encourages less experienced students to continue. Critics argue that a trophy loses meaning if it does not represent achievement.

Learning to lose can teach resilience, honesty and respect for stronger opponents, but constant pressure to win may encourage anxiety or cheating. Schools must decide which activities should remain competitive, how effort should be recognised and whether awards can celebrate progress without pretending that every result is the same.

A sports day committee has proposed participation medals for younger pupils and performance trophies for older teams. Coaches believe beginners need encouragement, whereas several students say honest results make improvement more satisfying.

The revised award system could recognise sportsmanship, persistence and personal progress alongside first place. Competitive events would remain, but teachers would review activities that repeatedly exclude less experienced players or place excessive pressure on a single child.

context.title: Practice context: Emoticons as Word of the Year
body: An emoticon was selected as a Word of the Year, reflecting how often people now use pictures in digital messages. Emoticons can show tone quickly, cross language barriers and make informal communication warmer. Their meaning, however, may change across cultures, age groups and situations.

A message made only of pictures can be unclear, and frequent informal use may not prepare students for careful writing. At the same time, languages have always changed as new tools appear. The question is whether picture-based communication supplements words or gradually replaces skills people still need.

Editors chose a “face with tears of joy” because it appeared in millions of messages and represented a major change in everyday communication. The decision was widely discussed precisely because the winning item was an image rather than a conventional word.

Teachers note that students already switch between formal essays and informal chats. Misunderstandings are most likely when an unfamiliar symbol carries different meanings for different readers, suggesting that context and audience remain important even in very short messages.

context.title: Practice context: Meditation in Secondary Schools
body: Meditation programmes teach students to sit quietly, focus on breathing and notice thoughts without reacting immediately. Some schools believe short sessions could reduce stress, improve concentration and help students manage emotions during demanding school days.

Results depend on good instruction and voluntary, respectful participation. Students may feel embarrassed, consider the practice a waste of time or connect it with beliefs they do not share. Schools also need time, space and trained staff. Meditation should therefore be judged as one possible well-being tool rather than a cure for every problem.

A six-week school trial would offer ten minutes of guided practice before afternoon lessons. Participation records would not affect grades, and students uncomfortable with closing their eyes could use a quiet breathing or listening exercise instead.

Counsellors will collect anonymous feedback on stress and concentration, while teachers record whether the transition into lessons becomes calmer. The trial will stop if sessions create discomfort or replace professional support needed by students with serious mental-health concerns.

context.title: Practice context: Twins in Schools
body: A school project is exploring the experiences of twins. Twins may share a close relationship and similar appearance, but they are still individuals with different interests, abilities and personalities. School practices can either recognise this individuality or encourage constant comparison.

The project could examine whether twins prefer the same class, how parents and teachers avoid confusing them and what advantages or difficulties they experience. Students will need reliable information from interviews, surveys and published research, then choose a presentation format that is informative without treating twins as a curiosity.

The project team plans confidential interviews with twins, parents and teachers from several year groups. Questions will cover classroom placement, mistaken identity, competition and whether people expect twins to share friends or interests.

Findings could be presented through paired audio clips, charts and short profiles in which each twin approves the final wording. Names and photographs would be optional, helping the exhibition challenge assumptions without exposing private family experiences.

context.title: Practice context: Students on Social Media
body: Students use social media to share photos, maintain friendships and express identity. A carefully chosen post can create a positive impression, but constant comparison and pressure for approval may affect confidence. Tags and images can also spread beyond the audience originally intended.

Acceptable behaviour includes asking permission, protecting private information and responding respectfully. Schools should help students think about lasting digital footprints without monitoring every conversation. Young people need practical strategies for dealing with unwanted tags, misleading images, online pressure and disagreements that move between screens and school life.

The counselling team has received reports of embarrassing photographs being reposted after the original uploader deleted them. Other students describe anxiety when popular classmates appear to have perfect social lives every day.

A peer-led campaign would demonstrate privacy settings, permission before tagging and ways to report harmful content. It would also remind viewers that edited posts show selected moments, not a complete measure of someone’s friendships, appearance or success.

body: A Bicycle Club is preparing a safety talk and comparing several cycling gadgets. Lights, reflective equipment, helmets and wearable signals may reduce risk, but no product can replace attention, road knowledge and responsible behaviour. Some gadgets may be expensive or uncomfortable.

The club should judge each item by effectiveness, ease of use, price and suitability for Hong Kong conditions. Its two recommendations need clear reasons and should form part of wider advice about checking a bicycle, choosing safe routes, following traffic rules and responding to pedestrians and other road users.

Four advertised products include a bright wheel light, an inflatable helmet, a handlebar direction signal and a jacket with reflective panels. The products address different dangers, so choosing two requires attention to both visibility and head protection.

Club members will compare independent safety testing rather than promotional claims. Their talk will also cover braking distance, hand signals and route planning, because a gadget that is poorly fitted or distracts its rider can create a new hazard.

Local writers welcome a new way to reach the public but want clear payment and selection arrangements. Librarians suggest printing a code linking each extract to borrowed books, author events and accessible electronic versions for readers who need larger text.

context.title: Practice context: International Left-Handers Day
body: International Left-Handers Day draws attention to everyday objects and routines designed mainly for right-handed people. Desks, scissors, tools and sports instruction can create small but repeated frustrations. Awareness can help schools notice barriers that right-handed students may never see.

An event could include demonstrations, adapted equipment and activities in which participants try common tasks with their non-dominant hand. Organisers should avoid stereotypes that all left-handed people are more creative or athletic. The purpose is practical inclusion and understanding, not turning a natural difference into a performance.

Students have found that several classroom desks and computer mice are uncomfortable for left-handed users. The school can borrow adapted sports equipment and invite a designer to explain why products should be tested by people with different needs.

The organising team proposes a lunchtime exhibition, a handwriting station and a review of school equipment. Activities will focus on practical barriers and solutions; claims about personality or intelligence will be labelled as myths unless supported by reliable evidence.

part_a.instruction: Today is International Left-Handers Day. Your group is organising activities for the day at your school. You may want to talk about:

discussion_points.text: Some of the frustrations that left-handed people experience
How these difficulties can be overcome
Activities you may organise for the event
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: Do you know any left-handed people?
How well can you use your left hand?
Can you use both hands and both feet equally well?
Do you think it would be a good idea to celebrate International Left-Handers Day?
Do you think left-handers have an advantage in sports?
Do you think left-handers are more creative than right-handers?
Do you think left-handed children should be forced to become right-handed?
Do you think all children should be taught to use both hands well at an early age?

context.title: Practice context: Texting Lanes
body: Some cities have experimented with marked lanes for people who text while walking. The idea attracts attention to distracted pedestrians, who may miss traffic signals, obstacles and other people. Yet a special lane may appear to approve the risky behaviour it is meant to reduce.

A texting lane is also difficult to enforce and may be ignored by the people paying least attention. Public messages, safer street design, school education and personal habits could be more effective. Any campaign should explain the danger clearly and encourage people to stop moving before using a phone.

A temporary lane in another city attracted photographs but little consistent use. Observers found that distracted walkers crossed the markings whenever crowds formed, while pedestrians without phones sometimes used the empty space.

The Student Union is considering floor signs at school exits, short videos based on real near-misses and designated stopping places away from crossings. Success would be measured by safer behaviour, not by how many people notice a colourful lane.

part_a.instruction: Your group is part of the Student Union and you are discussing ways to raise awareness about texting while walking. You may want to talk about:

discussion_points.text: The problems caused by using smartphones while walking
Whether texting lanes can help to solve these problems
Other ways of making people aware of the dangers of texting while walking
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: Do you use your smartphone while you are walking?
Would you walk in a texting lane?
Why do people use their smartphones while they are walking?
Are you aware of your surroundings when you use your smartphone?
Do you think texting lanes should be created in Hong Kong?
Should people be punished if they do not use the texting lanes?
Do you think the problem of texting while walking will get worse?
How would your phone habits be different if it was illegal to use smartphones while walking?
